name: West and South Sikkim
meta_description: Plan West and South Sikkim on a fair budget: Pelling, Yuksom, Ravangla, Namchi, Goecha La, monasteries, shared jeeps, stays and the true stories behind them.
summary: West and South Sikkim is where the Sikkimese kingdom began, at Yuksom in 1642, and where Kangchenjunga feels closest. Pelling and Ravangla are the bases, Yuksom the trailhead for Goecha La, and Namchi and Temi the gentle south. October to May is best; shared jeeps keep it affordable.
intro: This is the old heart of Sikkim. The first Chogyal was crowned at Yuksom in 1642, his son moved the court to Rabdentse above Pelling in 1670, and the oldest monasteries of the kingdom still stand on the same ridges: Dubdi, Pemayangtse, Sanga Choeling and Tashiding. Since 2021 the area falls in three districts, Gyalshing, Soreng and Namchi, but most travellers still call it West and South Sikkim.

Pelling, at about 2,150 m, is the base for the classic view of Kangchenjunga and for the monastery circuit. Yuksom, an hour and a half beyond, is the quiet village where the Goecha La trek begins. In the south, Ravangla has the 130-foot Buddha Park, Namchi has two giant statues on facing hills, and Temi is Sikkim's own tea estate. Further west, Rinchenpong, Uttarey and the Sherpa village of Okhrey lead to the rhododendron forests of Barsey.

It is also one of the easiest parts of the eastern Himalaya to do well on a modest budget. Shared jeeps and SNT buses link every town to Siliguri, Gangtok and Darjeeling. Village homestays cost a fraction of Pelling's resorts. Most sights are monasteries, lakes and walks that cost little or nothing to enter. The money goes on transport, so planning the order of your stops matters more than anywhere else.

We plan trips here around three seasons. October to December brings the clearest mountains. March to May brings rhododendrons and warmer nights. January and February are cold, clear and cheap. From June to September the monsoon closes the views and the roads slip, which is when hotels drop their rates and only the Tendong and Pang Lhabsol festivals draw crowds.

story.title: Three lamas, a churn of milk and a stone throne
paras: In 1641 and 1642 three Tibetan lamas of the Nyingma school made their way into Sikkim from different directions: Lhatsun Chenpo, Ngadak Sempa Chenpo and Kathok Rigzin Chenpo. They met in the Rathong Chu valley at a place the Lepchas came to call Yuksom, which Wikipedia's history of Sikkim renders as 'the place where the three monks met'. Their task, as they understood it, was to find the man who would rule the hidden land as a Buddhist king.

Tradition says Guru Rinpoche had foretold that the fourth man would come from the east. The lamas found Phuntsog Namgyal near present-day Gangtok, churning milk, and recognised him as the chosen one. Whatever the truth of the milk churn, the record is firm on the next part: in 1642, aged 38, Phuntsog Namgyal was crowned the first Chogyal of Sikkim on a stone seat under a pine at Norbugang, and anointed with water from a sacred urn.

The throne still stands at Yuksom, four stone seats with the highest kept for Lhatsun Chenpo, under a huge old cryptomeria. Opposite is the Norbugang Chorten, said to hold earth and water from every part of Sikkim. The Namgyal dynasty that began here lasted until 1975, when Sikkim joined India. You can walk to the throne from Yuksom's main road in fifteen minutes, and in the early morning you will often have it to yourself.
story.source: Wikipedia: Yuksom, Phuntsog Namgyal, Norbugang Chorten, History of Sikkim; the milk-churning story is tradition, not documented history

did_you_know: Yuksom was Sikkim's first capital from 1642, and in 1670 the second Chogyal, Tensung Namgyal, moved the court to Rabdentse, whose ruins stand near Pelling.
Joe Brown and George Band, who made the first ascent of Kangchenjunga on 25 May 1955, stopped a few feet short of the summit to keep a promise to Sikkim's ruler that the top would stay untrodden.
The 130-foot Buddha statue at Ravangla's Buddha Park was consecrated by the 14th Dalai Lama on 25 March 2013.
Temi Tea Garden, set up in 1969 under Sikkim's last Chogyal, Palden Thondup Namgyal, covers about 177 hectares on the slopes below Tendong hill.
Khangchendzonga National Park, which the Goecha La trek crosses from Yuksom, was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.
facts: Oct – Dec and Mar – May; Jan – Feb for clear, cold, cheap

highlights.title: Kangchenjunga from Pelling
highlights.text: On a clear morning between October and February the whole range lifts out of the dark above Pelling: Kangchenjunga at 8,586 m, Kabru, Pandim and their neighbours. Watch from Upper Pelling, Pemayangtse or the Rabdentse ridge. It costs nothing, and the best light lasts about twenty minutes after sunrise.

highlights.title: The monastery trail
highlights.text: Dubdi, Norbugang, Pemayangtse, Rabdentse, Sanga Choeling, Khecheopalri and Tashiding form Sikkim's oldest pilgrimage circuit, all within a day's drive of each other. Three or four days by car, or a week by shared jeep, covers them at an unhurried pace with time to sit through prayers.

highlights.title: Yuksom and Goecha La
highlights.text: Yuksom is where Sikkim's first king was crowned and where trekkers set off for Dzongri and Goecha La inside Khangchendzonga National Park. Even if you do not trek, two quiet nights here, with walks to Norbugang and Dubdi, are among the best value days in Sikkim.

highlights.title: Ravangla, Namchi and Temi
highlights.text: The south is gentler and closer to Siliguri. Ravangla's Buddha Park and Ralang Monastery, Namchi's Samdruptse statue of Guru Padmasambhava and the Char Dham complex, and the slopes of Temi Tea Garden make an easy three-day loop for families and older travellers.

highlights.title: Barsey rhododendrons
highlights.text: From mid-March to April the Barsey sanctuary on the Singalila range turns red and pink with rhododendron. A gentle 4 km walk from Hilley reaches the ridge, and Sherpa homestays in Okhrey make a cheap, friendly base. On clear days Kangchenjunga stands over the flowers.

highlights.title: Villages and homestays
highlights.text: Rinchenpong and Kaluk, Uttarey near the Nepal border, Darap, Khecheopalri and Okhrey offer homestays with home-cooked food at a fraction of Pelling's resort prices. Expect Limbu, Lepcha, Bhutia and Sherpa households, cardamom fields, quiet nights and very early mornings.

getting_there: The usual gateway is Siliguri: New Jalpaiguri (NJP) station or Bagdogra airport (IXB). From there Pelling is about 140–150 km and 5–6.5 hours by road via Sevoke, Melli, Jorethang, Legship and Gyalshing; Ravangla is about 120 km and Namchi about 100 km. Shared jeeps and a daily SNT bus leave Siliguri in the morning; reserved cars wait at NJP and Bagdogra. From Gangtok, Pelling is about 120 km and five hours via Ravangla or Rorathang. From Darjeeling, the shortest road drops to Jorethang on the Rangeet, about 75 km and 4–5 hours to Pelling. Pakyong airport near Gangtok has had limited and irregular flights; check current status before you travel. Arrive in the morning if you plan to use shared jeeps, as most leave before early afternoon.
permits: Indian nationals need no permit for Pelling, Yuksom, Ravangla, Namchi, Rinchenpong, Uttarey, Okhrey or Barsey; carry photo ID for checkposts. Foreign nationals need a Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, free and valid for 30 days, applied for online through e-FRRO or issued at the Melli and Rangpo checkposts. The Goecha La and Dzongri trek lies inside Khangchendzonga National Park: you pay park entry at the Yuksom forest checkpost and must trek with a registered agency and licensed guide; foreign nationals need a trek permit arranged by the agency. Rules and fees change, so check current status before you travel.

budget.summary: West Sikkim rewards slow, shared travel. Use shared jeeps and SNT buses for the long transfers from Siliguri, Gangtok or Darjeeling and hire cars only for sightseeing days, ideally split with other travellers. Stay in village homestays at Yuksom, Khecheopalri, Darap, Rinchenpong or Okhrey, where dinner and breakfast are often included. Most monasteries, lakes and walks are free or cost under ₹100. Travel in January–February or early December for clear skies at off-season rates.
tips: Arrive in Siliguri by mid-morning so you can catch a shared jeep instead of paying for a reserved car.
Base yourself in Upper Pelling and walk to Rabdentse, Sanga Choeling and Pemayangtse rather than hiring a car for them.
Share a sightseeing car with travellers from your hotel for the Khecheopalri–Yuksom day; four people cut the cost to a quarter.
Book homestays directly by phone in the off-season and ask for a meals-included rate.
Avoid the Puja and Diwali weeks in October and the Christmas–New Year week, when rates in Pelling can double.

months.weather: Pelling 0–10 °C, dry, frosty mornings, very clear
months.summary: January is cold, clear and quiet. Mornings in Pelling are often frosty and the range is sharp against a deep blue sky. Snow can dust Ravangla's upper slopes and Barsey. Goecha La is out of season. The Maghe Sankranti mela fills Jorethang's riverbank in mid-month, and the monastery circuit is peaceful. Shared jeeps run normally and roads are dry, so it is an easy month to travel cheaply.
months.tip: Pack thermals and a down jacket; many rooms rely on small heaters.
months.price_note: After the New Year week, rates fall to some of the lowest of the year and walk-in bargains are common.

months.weather: Pelling 1–12 °C, mostly dry and clear, cold nights
months.summary: February stays cold but the days lengthen. The Pemayangtse Cham dances close the Tibetan year, and Bumchu at Tashiding sometimes falls at the end of the month. Views are still reliable in the mornings. A good month for monasteries and village stays, with few crowds. Nights drop close to freezing in Pelling and Yuksom, so check that your room has a heater or plenty of blankets. Roads are dry and shared jeeps run on time.
months.tip: Check the Tibetan calendar dates for the Cham and Bumchu before you book.
months.price_note: Off-season rates hold except around festival days at Tashiding, when rooms nearby fill.

months.weather: Pelling 5–16 °C, clear mornings, haze builds by afternoon
months.summary: Spring starts. Rhododendrons begin to open on the Barsey ridge and along the trail above Yuksom by mid-month. Bumchu at Tashiding often falls in early March. Mornings are still good for Kangchenjunga, afternoons hazier. Trekking agencies start Goecha La departures late in the month. Temperatures are kind for walking, and the first village homestays reopen their gardens. It is a good month to pair Pelling with Okhrey and Barsey.
months.tip: Plan Barsey for late March or April for the fullest bloom.
months.price_note: Shoulder season: fair prices, though Okhrey homestays fill on peak bloom weekends.

months.summary: April is rhododendron month. Barsey and the forests below Dzongri are in bloom, Goecha La treks are in full swing, and Temi's first flush is on the bushes. Views come and go with the haze, so early starts matter. It is a lovely month for walking. Days are mild enough for long walks at Yuksom and Rinchenpong, and evenings still need a fleece. Hotels fill from the middle of the month.
months.tip: Be at viewpoints by sunrise; spring haze usually closes the view by mid-morning.
months.price_note: Prices rise from mid-April as school holidays begin in eastern India.

months.summary: May is warm and busy with families from the plains. Rhododendrons linger at higher levels, Goecha La departures continue, and the south around Ravangla and Namchi is green and pleasant. Pre-monsoon showers grow through the month, and mountain views become less reliable. Temi's second flush is on the bushes and the south is pleasant for families. Keep afternoons flexible for showers and plan viewpoints for dawn.
months.tip: Book hotels early for May; school-holiday weeks fill Pelling and Ravangla.
months.price_note: Peak season pricing in Pelling and Ravangla; homestays in Uttarey or Okhrey stay better value.

months.summary: The monsoon arrives in June. Rain and cloud hide the range most days, and landslides start on the roads through Melli, Jorethang and Legship. Waterfalls such as Kanchenjunga Falls are at their fullest. Goecha La treks stop. Only travel if you are flexible and want quiet. Hotels cut rates sharply and the villages are green and empty. Travel early in the day, keep the plan loose and do not book tight flight connections.
months.tip: Keep a spare day in your plan for road closures.
months.price_note: Deep discounts at most hotels, often 30–50% off rack rates.

months.summary: July is the wettest stretch. Roads slip often and views are rare. The hills are intensely green and the villages quiet. We only suggest July for travellers with plenty of time, a reserved car and no fixed flights. Leeches are out on every forest path, and many trekking agencies close for the season. Homestays welcome the few guests who come, often with long-stay discounts.
months.tip: Carry leech socks and a proper rain jacket for any walk.
months.price_note: Lowest rates of the year; ask for long-stay discounts.

months.summary: Still monsoon, but two festivals bring the south to life: Tendong Lho Rumfaat on 8 August and, in some years, Pang Lhabsol at the end of the month in Ravangla. Go for the culture rather than the views, and expect slides on the roads. Ravangla and Namchi are the best bases. The countryside is at its greenest and paddy fields shine in the valleys between showers.
months.tip: Base yourself in Ravangla or Namchi to reach both festivals easily.
months.price_note: Off-season rates, though Ravangla rooms tighten during the Pang Lhabsol week.

months.weather: Pelling 13–20 °C, rain easing late in the month
months.summary: The monsoon eases through September. Pang Lhabsol often falls in the first half of the month in Ravangla. By late September the first clear mornings return, waterfalls are still full, and hotels have not yet raised rates for the Puja season. Nights are mild, the hills are still green and the first trekking groups return to Yuksom by the end of the month. Keep one spare day for late monsoon slides.
months.tip: Late September is a smart value window before October prices.
months.price_note: Still off-season pricing until the Puja holidays begin.

months.summary: October is the classic month: clear skies, crisp mornings and Kangchenjunga on show almost daily. Goecha La treks run at their peak. It is also the Durga Puja and Diwali season, so Pelling, Yuksom and Ravangla are at their busiest. Sunrise from Upper Pelling is close to guaranteed in the second half of the month. Book early for Goecha La; agencies fill their departures well in advance.
months.tip: Book transport and rooms well ahead for the Puja weeks.
months.price_note: Highest prices of the year during Puja and Diwali weeks; book early.

months.summary: November is our favourite month. Views are as good as October with fewer crowds, Himalayan cherry blooms along the Temi approach road, and late Goecha La departures still run in good years. Nights turn cold, so pack warm. Temi's estate roads glow pink under the blossom while the hills turn gold and brown. Days are dry and roads are in good shape after the monsoon repairs.
months.tip: Go to Temi in November for cherry blossom and tea-garden views of the range.
months.price_note: Rates ease after Diwali; good value for clear weather.

months.summary: December brings cold, clear days and long views. The monastery circuit is calm, villages are quiet and the light is beautiful. Christmas and New Year weeks bring a short spike in visitors from Kolkata and beyond. Mornings bring the sharpest views of the year, often clear all day. Before the holiday week, rooms are easy to find and drivers have time for longer sightseeing days.
months.tip: Pack serious winter layers; nights in Okhrey and Yuksom go below freezing.
months.price_note: Good value until about 20 December, then peak rates through New Year.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Pelling and West Sikkim
faqs.a: October to December gives the clearest views of Kangchenjunga, and March to May brings rhododendrons and pleasant days. January and February are cold but very clear and cheap. Avoid June to August if views matter, because monsoon cloud and landslides are common. Late September is a good value window as the rains ease.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for West Sikkim
faqs.a: Four to five nights covers Pelling and Yuksom with the monastery circuit and Khecheopalri Lake. Add two nights for Ravangla, Namchi and Temi in the south. The Goecha La trek needs 9 to 11 days on its own. If you are combining with Gangtok and Darjeeling, plan at least seven nights.

faqs.q: Do Indians need a permit for Pelling or Yuksom
faqs.a: No. Indian nationals need only a photo ID for Pelling, Yuksom, Ravangla, Namchi and the villages. The exception is the Goecha La trek, which needs a Khangchendzonga National Park permit through a registered agency. Foreign nationals need a free Sikkim Restricted Area Permit. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I get from NJP to Pelling cheaply
faqs.a: Take an auto to the Siliguri jeep stands near the SNT terminus and buy a shared jeep seat to Gyalshing or Pelling for about ₹400–550, indicative, or catch the daily SNT bus for around ₹300–400. Leave in the morning; most jeeps go before early afternoon. From Gyalshing local jeeps reach Pelling in 25 minutes.

faqs.q: Is Pelling or Ravangla better for Kangchenjunga views
faqs.a: Pelling is closer to the main range and gives the classic, wide view from Upper Pelling, Pemayangtse and Rabdentse. Ravangla's view is good but more distant. For the closest view of all you need to trek to Dzongri, or stay in Yuksom and walk up towards Dubdi on a clear morning.

faqs.q: Can I do the Goecha La trek on my own
faqs.a: No. The trek runs through Khangchendzonga National Park and must be done with a registered trekking agency and a licensed guide; permits are arranged at Yuksom. Group departures with agencies cost about ₹14,000–25,000 per person, indicative, while a private trek costs much more. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is West Sikkim good for a family trip
faqs.a: Yes, if you keep drives short. Split the journey from Siliguri with a night in Ravangla or Namchi, base yourself in Pelling for three nights, and choose easy walks such as Rabdentse and the Buddha Park. Avoid the Puja and May school-holiday peaks if you can, since rooms and cars cost more then.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest way to see West Sikkim
faqs.a: Use shared jeeps and SNT buses between towns, stay in homestays with meals, walk to the sights near Pelling, and share a car with other travellers for the Yuksom–Khecheopalri day. Travel in January–February or early December. A careful traveller can manage on about ₹2,000–2,500 a day, indicative, excluding the trip from home.

faqs.q: Which is the oldest monastery in Sikkim
faqs.a: Dubdi Monastery, above Yuksom, established in 1701, is described as the oldest surviving monastery in Sikkim. Pemayangtse near Pelling was founded as a small temple in 1647 and enlarged in 1705, and Tashiding's site dates to 1641. All three are on the West Sikkim monastery trail and can be visited in two or three days.
